about: Verified research sizes for ten outcome-web links (Oct. 29, 2026). These sizes calibrate links a later family wires; no link reads them yet, and links.json is unchanged. One entry per researched source, each naming its link and what it is for (use). value and range are in the unit linkUnit states, which for a size is the link's own unit from links.json (the proportional change in the outcome per unit of the cause, unless linkUnit says otherwise); where the verifier corrected a value, range or lag, the corrected one is recorded. tag is SOURCED (the page prints it for this measure) or ESTIMATED (derived from the nearest study, with the source and spread). verified is true only where the verifier found the quote word for word and the conversion right; otherwise verifierProblem says what the verifier found wrong. A null value or range means the source prints no size for this link. The plain-English note is docs/research/evidence/outcome-web-sizes-2026-10-29.md; the plan is docs/reports/effects-web-plan-2026-10-29.md and the per-link survey docs/reports/effects-web-survey-2026-10-29.json. entries.citation: Collinson, Humphries, Mader, Reed, Tannenbaum and van Dijk (2024), 'Eviction and Poverty in American Cities', Quarterly Journal of Economics 139(1):57-120, Table VIII 'Impact on Hospital Use' (New York sample, judge-leniency IV). Read in the accepted QJE manuscript (Cowles PDF) and in NBER Working Paper 30382 (Aug. 2022, rev. July 2023, https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w30382/w30382.pdf); both print the same Table VIII and the same sentence.
entries.quote: Table VIII: Impact on Hospital Use ... 1-4 Quarters After Filing: E[Y |E = 0] / OLS / IV ... "Number of hospital visits 0.739 0.055*** 0.188** 0.632 0.039*** -0.113" with standard errors "(1.321) (0.006) (0.094) (1.208) (0.006) (0.142)". Text, section VI.E: "In the first year after the case, eviction increases total hospital visits by 0.19 visits in the first year following the case (29 percent relative to the non-evicted mean)." Table notes: "'Number of hospital visits' is the total number of non-pregnancy-related hospital visits."
entries.linkUnit: From housing.eviction to health.hospital-visits, per 'eviction order' (one evicted tenant), shape linear, lagMonths 0. Size is the proportional change in one evicted tenant's own non-pregnancy hospital visits per eviction order (links.json 'about').
entries.conversion: 1) IV effect, quarters 1-4 after filing: +0.188 non-pregnancy hospital visits per evicted tenant, SE 0.094 (Table VIII col 3). 2) Base: the non-evicted mean over the same quarters is 0.739 visits (col 1). 3) Ratio = 0.188 / 0.739 = 0.2544, so visits are multiplied by 1.254 in the 12 months after filing. 4) 95% CI of the effect = 0.188 +/- 1.96 x 0.094 = [0.00376, 0.37224]; divided by 0.739 that is [0.0051, 0.5037]. 5) Year two (quarters 5-8): -0.113 (SE 0.142) on a base of 0.632 = -0.179, CI [-0.619, +0.262]. That is not significant, so the size after month 12 is 0, not a reversal. 6) The text's '29 percent' does not come out of the table: 0.188/0.739 = 25.4% and 0.19/0.739 = 25.7%; 29% would need a base of about 0.648, which neither paper prints. The table numbers are used, and 0.29 falls inside the range.
entries.caveats: Applies to compliers (marginal filed-case tenants under random judge assignment) in New York only. The base is non-evicted tenants with a filed case, whose visits were already rising before filing, not the general population; the base is the mean for every such tenant while 0.188 is a complier effect, a mix the paper itself makes, so the ratio is approximate (the base's SE, about 0.003, is small enough to ignore). The window is counted from case filing, not the order, and covers quarters 1-4 only: the health engine's healthEvictionEffectDays is 730 (parameters.json:5065), so a care multiplier read in careNeedOf (health.ts:1059) should apply for 365 days. The size multiplies one evicted tenant's own non-pregnancy hospital use; it must not go on a place-level health.hospital-visits ledger, and if careNeedOf counts pregnancy care, only the non-pregnancy part is scaled. Emergency visits alone: 0.106/0.588 = 0.180, CI [-0.116, 0.477], not significant. Mental-health visits: 0.054/0.047 = 1.15 (p<0.1). healthEvictionHazardFactor 1.1 (parameters.json:5053) was inferred from this same study's health-care results, and care used and strain are two outcomes: the year-one visit effect must not be counted in both. The QJE text's 29% conflicts with its own Table VIII; the table is used. Verifier: quote found word for word in both PDFs (the QJE copy prints '1–4 Quarters' with an en dash); arithmetic and the repository facts above confirmed.

entries.use: The size in the per-service unit the planned build moves to (proportional change in service per resident), for transit commuters.
entries.citation: Bastiaanssen, Johnson and Lucas (2020), 'Does transport help people to gain employment? A systematic review and meta-analysis of the empirical evidence', Transport Reviews 40(5):607-628, doi 10.1080/01441647.2020.1747569 (accepted version, White Rose Research Online record https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/158809/). Wait times from the National Household Travel Survey via Governing (https://www.governing.com/archive/gov-transit-driving-times.html) and from Moovit via Metro Magazine (https://www.metro-magazine.com/10037552/u-s-commuters-wait-approximately-40-mins-a-day-for-public-transit).
entries.quote: "The various public transport access and job accessibility measures used in studies were found incompatible with each other and thus were unsuitable for a meta-regression." Abstract: "While our systematic review suggests that better access to public transport and higher levels of job accessibility increases employment probabilities, meta-regression analysis requires more consistent transport measures." Section 4.2, commute time: "The overall random effect of the meta-regression shows a small negative sign of -0.014*** with a related odds-ratio of 0.986, 95% CI [0.985, 0.988], p<0.001, which indicates that as the mean commute times increase, the odds of employment slightly decreases" | Governing: "Wait times for all transit trips nationally average around 10 minutes, according to the latest data from the Department of Transportation's National Household Travel Survey." | Metro Magazine: "People in major U.S. cities wait approximately 40 minutes per day for public transit ... This accounts for 31% of their commute time."
entries.linkUnit: From transit.service-access to labor.unemployment-pct, shape linear, lagMonths 0. The row's per today is 'line lost'; the survey's planned build re-expresses it per proportional change in service per resident, so this value is the proportional change in unemployment-pct per unit proportional cut in service, for the transit-dependent group.
entries.conversion: The paper prints no pooled public-transport effect (quote 1). Its nearest pooled number is commute time: log-odds -0.014 per minute of mean neighborhood commute, OR CI [0.985, 0.988], so beta is in [-0.01511, -0.01207]. 1) Logit to unemployment: du/dx = -beta x (1-u) x u, so the proportional change in u per minute = |beta| x (1-u). At the links.json baseline u = 4%: 0.014 x 0.96 = 0.01344 per minute, CI [0.01159, 0.01451]. 2) Service to minutes: a proportional service cut s on the same routes raises headway by s/(1-s), about s, and mean wait rises in proportion, so added minutes = W x s, with W = 10 (NHTS via Governing) to 20 (Moovit's 40 minutes a day over 2 one-way trips). 3) Size = 0.01344 x 10 = 0.134 per unit proportional service cut (a 10% cut gives +1.3% on the unemployment rate). 4) Range (verifier's correction for an all-ages group): the -0.014 is youth-driven (Table 4: youth on 66 of 71 observations, adjustment -0.021); by footnote 9 the non-youth pooled log-odds is about ln(0.976) + 0.021 = -0.0033 per minute (the verifier's derivation; the paper does not print it, and Table 4's constant -0.001, p 0.781, agrees), so the floor is 0.0033 x 0.96 x 10 = 0.032. The top stays 0.01451 x 20 = 0.290. The point value 0.134 stands as the youth-weighted estimate.
entries.caveats: Bastiaanssen et al. publish no number for public transport; this value comes from their commute-time meta-regression of 8 US cross-sectional studies, mostly youth, no IV, so it reads as a long-run association. The regressor is the mean neighborhood one-way commute of workers, a job-access proxy, not one rider's added wait, and car commute times appear on 60 of 71 observations (the mode dummy is not significant). The logit is evaluated at employment 0.96 within the labor force; the studies model employed vs not employed in youth samples at a much lower rate, where the same odds ratio gives about 10 times the effect, so u = 4% is a plausible but unstated assumption (it agrees with Tyndall). Wait rising in proportion to headway holds for frequent service where riders arrive at random; for infrequent routes riders time their arrival, so it overstates. Moovit's page does not say whether its 40 minutes include transfers, so the 2-trip split is rough and serves as the upper end. Applies to transit commuters, the link's 'transit-dependent residents', not everyone in the place; car-owner effects are much smaller (Tyndall 0.7 vs 2.2 points). Cross-checks: Johnson et al. 2017 gives 0.152 area-wide (after the verifier's correction) and Tyndall 2017 gives 0.175 per line lost. Per the survey, read it at the jobs engine's decision only, never multiplied on the web's labor.unemployment-pct ledger, which eight built links read. Verifier: quotes found word for word (Governing dated Jan. 26, 2017, no survey year given; Metro Magazine Dec. 11, 2014); arithmetic correct.

entries.use: A cross-check on the per-service size, area-wide (all residents).
entries.citation: Johnson, Ercolani and Mackie (2017), 'Econometric analysis of the link between public transport accessibility and employment', Transport Policy 60:1-9, doi 10.1016/j.tranpol.2017.08.001 (accepted version, White Rose 120321). Cited in Bastiaanssen et al. 2020 sec. 3.3 as the England evidence; the nearest study that prints a usable coefficient.
entries.quote: Table 7-1 'Results of models by area type with employment rate as dependent variable': "ln(Bus T.T.) -0.016 -3.3 -0.019 -4.7 -0.012 -3.1 -0.010 -4.3" (coeff and t-stat for London, Dense Urban, Other Urban, Rural). Footnote 13: "The official employment rate is calculated as E/(E+U+I)". Conclusions: "The results suggest a difference of 10% in bus journey times between areas would be associated to 0.13-0.3% difference in employment depending on area type"
entries.linkUnit: transit.service-access to labor.unemployment-pct, shape linear, lagMonths 0. The value is the proportional change in unemployment-pct per unit proportional cut in service per resident, area-wide (all residents).
entries.conversion: As corrected by the verifier. 1) Table 7-1's dependent variable is the employment rate E/(E+U+I) as a fraction, not its log (section 2.1: 'proportional variables (such as car unavailability, gender mix) are not logged'; evaluated at the Table 3-3 means the model's fitted values, 0.697, 0.681, 0.713 and 0.750, match the observed rates 0.692, 0.674, 0.702 and 0.750). So each coefficient on ln(Bus T.T.) is the absolute change in the rate per log point of bus journey time: -0.016, -0.019, -0.012, -0.010 (London, Dense Urban, Other Urban, Rural). 2) Elasticity = coefficient / rate: 0.0231, 0.0282, 0.0171, 0.0133, mean 0.0204. 3) Service to journey time: a proportional cut s raises wait in proportion to headway; waiting is 31% of US commute time (Moovit) and 26% in New York City (same article: "38 minutes (26 percent) idly waiting"), so journey time rises by 0.31 x s (spread 0.26-0.31). 4) Employment to unemployment, if every lost job becomes unemployment (labor force fixed): delta u / u = |e| x (dT/T) x E/U; at u = 4%, E/U = 24. 5) Size = 24 x 0.31 x 0.0204 = 0.152. Spread of the point estimates: 24 x 0.26 x 0.0133 = 0.083 to 24 x 0.31 x 0.0282 = 0.210. With the confidence bounds: the widest lower bound is Other Urban, 0.012 - 1.96 x 0.00387 = 0.0044, divided by 0.702 = 0.0063, giving 24 x 0.26 x 0.0063 = 0.039; the upper bound is Dense Urban, 0.0269 / 0.674 = 0.0400, giving 24 x 0.31 x 0.0400 = 0.297.
entries.verifierProblem: The researcher's conversion read Table 7-1's coefficients as elasticities of the employment rate and gave 0.106, range [0.034, 0.200]. Table 7-1's dependent variable is the rate as a fraction, not its log, so the elasticity is coefficient / rate (mean 0.0204, not 0.01425): corrected value 0.152, range [0.039, 0.297]. Even under the first reading the CI floor would have been 0.028, not 0.034 (the widest lower bound is Other Urban, not Rural). The conclusions sentence '0.13-0.3% difference in employment' is about the employment level elasticities (Table 4-1, footnote 11), not Table 7-1.
entries.caveats: England, 2011 Census, Middle Layer Super Output Areas (MSOAs), cross-section with district fixed effects; IV tests found little endogeneity. It measures a long-run within-district difference, not a shock. It is area-wide, so it averages in car owners; for the transit-dependent group alone the slope is larger by roughly 1 / (their share of workers). Step 4 is an upper bound, because some lost jobs become inactivity rather than unemployment. Applying Moovit's US 31% wait share to the Department for Transport's modeled bus journey time to employment centers is an extra transfer assumption. The paper's text says a -0.016 parameter gives 'an uplift of a factor of 1.017'; that is wrong under either reading (under the level model -0.016 x ln(0.9) = +0.0017 on the rate, a factor of about 1.0024). The table coefficients are used.

entries.use: The size in the row's current unit, per line lost (the link's own source).
entries.citation: Tyndall (2017), 'Waiting for the R train: Public transportation and employment', Urban Studies 54(2):520-537, doi 10.1177/0042098015594079 (the link's own source). Read from the author's manuscript on his site; SAGE returned 403. The Urban Studies journal blog post of July 8, 2015 (https://urbanstudiesjnl.blogspot.com/2015/07) prints the same 1.4 points.
entries.quote: "After controls are in place, the estimated effect on an individual attributable to living adjacent to the R Train in 2013 is an increase in the probability of being unemployed of 1.4 percentage points (Table 2, column 5)." Table 2 col (5): "Adjacent to Brooklyn R Train in 2013 ... .014** (0.002)". Base: "Between 2010 and 2012 the rate of unemployment decreased significantly within the treatment neighborhoods, falling from 9.8% to 8.0%." Subgroups: "The effect on longer-term residents is only 1.1 percentage points." and "individuals without access to a vehicle were found to suffer a much larger increase of 2.2 percentage points."
entries.linkUnit: transit.service-access to labor.unemployment-pct, per 'line lost' (the row's current unit), shape linear, lagMonths 0; size = proportional change in the unemployment rate per line lost.
entries.conversion: 1) Difference-in-differences effect of losing the R line on adjacent Brooklyn neighborhoods, 2013: +0.014 probability unemployed (1.4 points), robust SE 0.002. 2) Base: those neighborhoods' 2012 unemployment rate was 8.0%. 3) Ratio = 0.014 / 0.080 = 0.175, so unemployment-pct is multiplied by 1.175 per line lost. 4) 95% CI = 0.014 +/- 1.96 x 0.002 = [0.01008, 0.01792]; divided by 0.080 that is [0.126, 0.224]. 5) Longer-term residents only, which removes self-selection by movers: 1.1 / 8.0 = 0.1375.
entries.caveats: One city, one line: the Montague Street Tunnel loss after Hurricane Sandy (Oct. 29, 2012), measured in the 2013 ACS. Timing (verifier's correction): the tunnel reopened Dec. 21, 2012; the long closure was announced June 5, 2013 and ran Aug. 2, 2013 to Sept. 14, 2014, during which 'the R Train was split into two routes'. So the 2013 ACS saw about 2 months of outage in late 2012 and about 5 in 2013, not a continuous loss; a full-year loss could be larger. Base choice: 8.0% is the 2012 pre-period rate; 2013 rose to 8.4%, so the without-closure 2013 rate is 8.4 - 1.4 = 7.0%, which gives 0.20, CI [0.144, 0.256], and the observed 8.4% gives 0.167; a fairer range is about [0.1375, 0.256]. The table's SEs are robust but not clustered, while treatment is assigned to three PUMAs, so the CI understates uncertainty. The treatment cut the direct link to Manhattan rather than removing every station, so 'line lost' is not a fixed share of service per resident; the survey found no study that converts it. Part of the effect is unemployed people moving in (recent movers +3.2 points, longer-term residents +1.1). By group: no vehicle +2.2 vs vehicle +0.7; Hispanic +3.4. The per-service values (Bastiaanssen chain 0.134, Johnson 0.152) are of the same order, but that comparison is loose: they are slopes per unit proportional cut (linearized; headway grows as s/(1-s), which diverges near s = 1) for transit commuters, against an all-workforce per-line effect.

entries.use: The size for this link (a deliberately conservative center, per enrollee).
entries.citation: Zuo, George W. 2021. "Wired and Hired: Employment Effects of Subsidized Broadband Internet for Low-Income Americans." American Economic Journal: Economic Policy 13(3): 447-82 (doi 10.1257/pol.20190648). The quote is the paper's own sentence as reprinted by Freethink, because the paper itself would not load: the author's working-paper PDF (econweb.umd.edu/~zuo/files/Broadband_Zuo_AEJ_Submit.pdf) returned HTTP 503 to WebFetch and a TLS chain error to curl, and the AEA article PDF is paywalled. The base comes from the official AEA online appendix (next entry).
entries.quote: Dr. Zuo explained in his study that the “availability of Internet Essentials led to a 0.9 percentage point increase (1.6 percent) in the probability that an eligible low-income individual was employed. After adjusting for take-up rates, I calculate that enrollees were 8.1 percentage points (14.3 percent) more likely to be employed.”
entries.linkUnit: Proportional change in labor.employment-rate per percentage point of households with home broadband (cause broadband.home-access, in percent of households), shape linear, lagMonths 0. The row's current per ('county gains broadband: +1.8 points') is not a slope; this uses the per that the survey and the sibling row broadband-to-married-women-work (size 0.0007 per point) already use.
entries.conversion: 1) Treatment on the treated: +8.1 points of employment per enrollee, which the paper calls +14.3%. The base is 8.1/0.143 = 0.566, which matches the appendix's 'Treatment group mean (2011) 0.567' (Table A8); the intent-to-treat check agrees: 0.009/0.567 = 1.59%, the paper's '1.6 percent'. 2) Treat an enrolling household as one that gains home broadband, following the Dettling row's 'household that gains access' convention: one point more of households with broadband is 1% of households x 14.3% = +0.143% of the employment rate, so the size is 0.00143 (rounded 0.0014). 3) Low end: the appendix prints no SE for the main 0.009, so it is estimated at about 0.0033 by pooling Table A12's male (SE 0.005) and female (SE 0.004) estimates by inverse variance (0.0031) and the education and age splits (0.0035). The ITT 95% interval is 0.009 +/- 1.96 x 0.0033 = [0.0025, 0.0155], 0.28x to 1.72x the point estimate, so 0.00143 x [0.28, 1.72] = [0.0004, 0.0025]. 4) High end raised to 0.0032 by the Wald cross-check (next entry): not every enrollee is a new subscriber (home internet use rose 0.049, take-up was 0.009/0.081 = 0.111, so about 0.44 new home-internet users per enrollee), which makes the effect per new subscriber larger than per enrollee. Final: size 0.0014, range [0.0004, 0.0032].
entries.caveats: (a) The study covers only adults in families at or under 185% of the poverty line with a school-age child; the AEA Research Highlight 'Expanding broadband access' (Oct. 6, 2021, https://www.aeaweb.org/research/charts/employment-internet-poor-americans) says: 'All the households in the sample had incomes below 185 percent of the federal poverty line. However, only families with a school-aged child were eligible for the program.' Putting the size on every household that gains broadband assumes those households resemble that group; in the game most households already subscribe (92.8% is the median of the 52 place rates in place-outcome-bases-2024.json, not a national share) and the rest skew low-income. Use the incomeFifth varies entry below. (b) The 2019 working-paper version (Zuo and Kolliner; abstract on the IPUMS Bibliography, https://bibliography.ipums.org/citations/show/14b84c74-b518-37dd-81db-8096b1b24992) reported 'Program enrollment increases the probability that an eligible lowincome individual is employed by 4.4 percentage points (7.8%)', a size of 0.00078, inside the range. (c) A WebSearch snippet of the author's PDF gave a TOT 'lower bound of 2.1 percentage points (3.7%)' (size 0.00037); that page would not load, so it is not used. (d) Possible double count with broadband-to-married-women-work (Dettling): Zuo finds the same effect for men and women (Table A12: 0.009 and 0.009, p = 0.963), so either leave partnered women out or net Dettling out. (e) Kolko 2012 finds no county-level employment-rate effect; the Atasoy +1.8 points is for a county gaining availability and cannot be converted to this unit. (f) Lag: the event study (Table A7) shows the effect building as enrollment grew (2012 0.005, 2013 0.010, 2014 0.015**, 2015 0.018***). Their simple mean is 0.012; the pooled DDD 0.009 is lower because it is measured against all pre-years (2009 0.003 and 2010 0.007 relative to 2011). The cause already carries a 36-month law-to-access lag in public-broadband-to-home-access, so lag 0 here is kept. (g) The 0.0033 SE is an estimate, not a printed figure; it pools subgroup SEs as if independent, though men and women share PUMA clusters, so the true SE may be larger (the urban and non-urban SEs give 0.0035, the yearly event-study SEs are 0.006); at SE 0.004 the low end would be about 0.0002. (h) Verifier: in the link's own unit the consistent per-new-subscriber figure is the Wald 0.0032, so 0.0014 is a deliberately conservative center, defended by Kolko's null; the row should say so. With the web's varies normalization (outcome-web-reach.ts scaled()), 0.0014 must be read as the national per-point average, which holds only if new subscribers come from the low-income fifths.

entries.citation: Zuo, George W. 2021. Online Appendix to "Wired and Hired", AEJ: Economic Policy 13(3): 447-82. Table A10 (effect of Internet Essentials availability on home internet use, CPS supplements, eligibles only) and Table A8 (treatment-group employment mean).

Outcome: Uses Internet at Home (% Comcast Coverage)×(Yr≥2012) 0.049** 0.039** 0.078*** 0.065*** (0.022) (0.017) (0.016) (0.013) ... Untreated mean 0.650 0.681 0.635 0.670 Low-income threshold (% of FPL) 185 250 185 250 Geographic Aggregation Metro Metro State State. [Table A8:] Treatment group mean (2011) 0.567
entries.linkUnit: Proportional change in labor.employment-rate per percentage point of households with home broadband (broadband.home-access, percent of households), shape linear, lagMonths 0.
entries.conversion: Both the employment effect and the internet-use effect are per 100% Comcast coverage among eligibles, so their ratio is the employment effect per point of home internet use. Column (1), the metro sample at the 185% FPL line: 0.009 / 0.049 = 0.184 points of employment per point of home internet use, or +18.4 points for each new home-internet user. As a proportion of the 0.567 base: 0.184 / 0.567 / 100 = 0.0032 per point of households. The other columns give 0.009/0.039 = 0.231 (size 0.0041), 0.009/0.078 = 0.115 (size 0.0020) and 0.009/0.065 = 0.138 (size 0.0024). Value 0.0032 (column 1), range [0.0020, 0.0041] across the four columns.
entries.caveats: A ratio of two separate regressions on different data, geography and design: employment from the ACS by PUMA as a DDD (eligibles vs low-income ineligibles), internet use from the CPS by metro or state as a DD among eligibles only. The like-for-like employment DD among eligibles (Table A8 Panel A, 0.013*** (0.003)) would give 0.0047 (column 1), about [0.0029, 0.0059] across the columns, but that DD moves with the control group (Panel B 0.006***), so the DDD numerator is the better choice; the Wald's sensitivity to it is why it serves only as the top of the range. The outcome is any home internet, not broadband only. The implied +18 points per new user (+32% relative) is large next to Kolko's null. The 0.009 numerator is the paper's figure as reprinted (previous entry), since the main Table 3 is paywalled.

entries.conversion: No page that loaded splits the effect by income inside the eligible group; the appendix splits by urban, sex, education and age, and any poverty-level split would be in the paywalled main text. The whole estimate is for families at or under 185% FPL. Recommended varies row by incomeFifth: the full effect on the fifths whose household income is at or under 185% of the poverty line, using the game's own income table for the shares, and zero above. By sex the weights are equal (0.009 vs 0.009, p = 0.963). Education (0.012 vs 0.007, p = 0.48) and age (0.012 vs 0.006, p = 0.40) differ but not significantly, so no weights are set. The results suggest that a ten-unit increase in ambient TSP exposure in the year of birth reduces average annual age 29-31 earnings by around 1 percent. [Table 4, Panel B: Annual Earnings] Mean TSPs (/10) -186.21 -286.83∗ -266.88∗ -351.74∗ (139.30) (158.61) (145.62) (190.39) [Text:] suggests that CAAA reduced TSP concentrations by 8-12 µg/m3. Relative to baseline earnings in nonattainment counties of $23,623 [NBER Digest:] a 10 percent decrease in TSPs in the year of birth is associated with a 1 percent increase in annual earnings at age 30.

entries.conversion: 1) Table 4 Panel B is dollars of mean annual earnings at ages 29-31 per 10 µg/m3 of TSP in the birth year. 2) Elasticity = (beta/10) x (mean TSP / mean earnings) = (beta/10) x (95.9 / 23,623). Column (4), all controls: (-351.74/10) x 0.0040596 = -0.143. Columns (1)-(3): -0.076, -0.116, -0.108. The inverse-SE-weighted mean of the four columns is -$266.58, or -0.108. The reduced-form check (footnote 22, $259 on $23,623 for about a 10% TSP drop) gives -0.11. The authors' and the NBER Digest's rounded statement (10% less TSP, 1% more earnings) is exactly -0.1. Value: -0.1. 3) 95% intervals, beta +/- 1.96 SE converted the same way: col (1) [-0.186, +0.035], col (2) [-0.243, +0.010], col (3) [-0.224, +0.008], col (4) [-0.294, +0.009]; the union is [-0.29, +0.04]. The 90% intervals exclude zero in columns (2)-(4): col (4) [-0.270, -0.016]. 4) An elasticity has no unit, so it carries from TSP to the game's PM2.5: a birth year 10% cleaner than base gives 0.9^(-0.1) = 1.0106, so +1.06% earnings at 30. 5) Cross-check: Panel C (log earnings, workers with positive earnings) col (4) -0.014 (0.008) per 10 units gives -0.014 x 95.9/10 = -0.134, 95% interval [-0.285, +0.016].
entries.caveats: (a) The paper measures TSP; 95.9 µg/m3 is Table 2's 1969 mean for nonattainment counties (attainment 58.59), the right base because it pairs with the nonattainment earnings base of $23,623, also from Table 2. The game's env.particulates is PM2.5 at about 8.8 µg/m3 nationally (America's Health Rankings, place-outcome-bases-2024.json). Carrying the elasticity over assumes PM2.5 moves in proportion to TSP and a constant elasticity at levels about ten times lower, which is why the tag is ESTIMATED. (b) The single-column 95% intervals include zero; the result is significant at 10% in columns (2)-(4). The authors call their estimates lower bounds ('We view these estimates as lower bounds on the true value due to several potential sources of bias that would attenuate our baseline estimates'). The range's top, +0.04, has the wrong sign (a dirtier birth year would raise earnings); it is kept as the statistically honest union, and [-0.29, 0] or the col-4 90% interval [-0.27, -0.02] are the sign-consistent alternatives. (c) Only the birth year matters: 'the lack of negative coefficients for cohorts born in 1969 and 1970 suggests that there are little to no differential benefits from exposure beginning at ages 1, 2, or 3', which supports per 'birth-year exposure'. (d) Effects are similar from 27 to 35 ('the confidence intervals overlap across all of them'), so the read can apply across working ages, not only at 30. (e) The published JPE numbers may differ slightly from the September 2014 NBER revision.

entries.citation: Barreca, Clay, Deschenes, Greenstone and Shapiro, 'Adapting to Climate Change: The Remarkable Decline in the U.S. Temperature-Mortality Relationship over the 20th Century', IZA Discussion Paper 8915 (March 2015), Table 3 Panel B (daily maximum temperature bins), column 3 (1960-2004), and the text on page 13. This is the revision that became JPE 124(1):105-159 (2016); the JPE full text returned 403 and the JPE abstract was read on IDEAS.
entries.quote: Table 3: Estimates of the Impact of High and Low Temperatures on Log Monthly Mortality Rate ... 1931-2004 1931-1959 1960-2004 ... Daily Maximum Temperature / Number of Days Above 100°F 0.0038*** 0.0052*** 0.0015* (0.0005) (0.0012) (0.0006) / Number of Days Between 90-99°F 0.0002 0.0002 0.0005 (0.0003) (0.0004) (0.0003). Also on page 13: "Over the 1900-1959 period the average annual mortality rate was 1,111 per 100,000 population, and this rate declined to an average of 885.8 over 1960-2004."
entries.linkUnit: From env.hot-days (days a year with a high of 90F or more, place-outcome-bases-2024.json) to health.heat-deaths, shape linear, per 'hot day', lagMonths 0. health.heat-deaths has no base or scale yet, so the value is excess deaths from hot days per 100,000 people a year per extra hot day; the proportional size follows from whatever base the outcome gets (step 6).
entries.conversion: 1) Each coefficient is the change in the log monthly mortality rate from one more day in that bin, summed over the hot month and the next, against a day with a high of 50-89F, holding the night's minimum-temperature bin fixed. 2) The game counts days with a high of 90F or more. Most are 90-99F days (0.0005) and the rest 100F-plus days (0.0015), so the central value uses 0.0005. 3) Extra deaths = coefficient x monthly death rate = 0.0005 x (885.8 / 12 = 73.82 per 100,000 a month) = 0.0369 per 100,000 per extra hot day; the 100F-plus bin gives 0.0015 x 73.82 = 0.111. 4) Range [0, 0.111]: from the 90-99F 95% CI (0.0005 +/- 1.96 x 0.0003 = [-0.0001, 0.0011]) floored at 0, to the 100F-plus bin's point estimate. For reference, the 90-99F CI tops out at 0.0011 x 73.82 = 0.081 and the 100F-plus CI at 0.198. 5) As a share of all deaths: 0.0005 / 12 = 0.0000417 of the place's annual all-cause rate per hot day, range [0, 0.000125]; because the coefficient is a log change, this form carries to today's death rates. 6) In the link's proportional unit, if health.heat-deaths keeps base H0 = 0.0369 x the place's base hot days, the size is 1 / base hot days: 0.0356 at the unweighted mean of the 50 states and D.C. (28.08 days), 0.0329 at the mean of all 56 places (30.40 days), from 1/99.8 = 0.010 at the highest place to 1/0.1 = 10 at the lowest (0.1 hot days). One linear size cannot hold that, so either set shape 'elasticity' with size 1.0 (the paper's model is linear in day counts) or put the outcome on a 'level' scale with size 0.037 per 100,000.
entries.caveats: The coefficients are SOURCED, but folding them into one 'high of 90F or more' day is ESTIMATED: the share of 100F-plus days among them was not read, and the max-temperature bins hold the night's minimum fixed (a 70-79F night adds 0.0006, SE 0.0005). Multiplying by the all-year average monthly death rate slightly overstates, because summer months run below the annual average. This 0.037 holds at the 1960-2004 average AC share of 59%. Because the web's AC moderator is absolute, the size it multiplies must be the zero-AC value: 0.0369 / (1 - 0.59) = 0.090 with the moderator capped at full protection (0.094 with the uncapped -1.03); see the moderator entry. Barreca finds larger per-day effects in cooler regions ('consistent with the idea that hotter places adapt'), so across places the elasticity is below 1, while within a place's year-to-year drift the linear form fits. Per the survey, only the change from base may count, because the SSA table and the 'other' death share already contain today's heat deaths. The NBER w18692 (2013) version prints slightly different numbers (0.0033 instead of 0.0034 for mean days over 90F, 1960-2004).

entries.citation: Deschenes and Greenstone (2011), 'Climate Change, Mortality, and Adaptation: Evidence from Annual Fluctuations in Weather in the US', American Economic Journal: Applied Economics 3(4):152-185: introduction (page 153), text (page 167) and Table 2 Panel A (page 168). Read from the published PDF hosted by UCSB's Broom Center; the AEA PDF returned 403 and MIT DSpace returned 429.
entries.quote: "For example, we find that an additional day with a mean temperature exceeding 90° F, relative to a day in the 50°–60° F range, leads to an increase in the annual age-adjusted mortality rate of about 0.11 percent." Table 2, Impact on annual mortality rate per 100,000, Days > 90° F (1d): "4. Age 65+ ... 5.219* (1.416)"; "5. Age-adjusted (population weighted average) 0.692* 0.587* 0.330 0.936* (0.323) (0.251) (0.207) (0.289)". Text: "The largest coefficient is the one associated with the >90° F temperature bin and it is 0.94."
entries.linkUnit: Same as the Barreca entry: env.hot-days (days with a high of 90F or more) to health.heat-deaths, linear, per hot day, lag 0; the value is excess deaths per 100,000 a year per extra hot-high day.
entries.conversion: 1) Printed: 0.936 more annual age-adjusted deaths per 100,000 (SE 0.289) per extra day with a MEAN temperature above 90F, against a 50-60F day, 1968-2002; 'about 0.11 percent' of the annual rate implies a base of 0.936 / 0.0011 = 851 per 100,000. 2) 95% CI: 0.936 +/- 1.96 x 0.289 = [0.370, 1.502]. 3) The game's hot day (a high of 90F or more) is far milder and more common: D&G Table 1 counts 1.39 days a year with a mean above 90F nationally, and Barreca et al. (IZA DP 8915, footnote 15) say 'On days where the daily mean temperature exceeds 90°F, the daily maximum temperature was 106 °F, on average.' To scale, use Barreca's 1960-2004 ratio of the per-day effect of a 90-99F-high day to a mean-above-90F day: 0.0005 / 0.0034 = 0.147. 4) 0.936 x 0.147 = 0.138 per 100,000 per hot-high day; as a share of all deaths 0.0011 x 0.147 = 0.00016. 5) Range (verifier's correction): the Barreca ratio is the largest uncertainty, since its numerator (0.0005, SE 0.0003) is not significant; its CI [-0.0001, 0.0011] makes the ratio [0, 0.32], so at the central D&G value the range is [0, 0.936 x 0.32 = 0.30] (with D&G's own CI as well, [0, 0.49]). 6) Proportional size: as in the Barreca entry, 1 / base hot days if the outcome's base is the slope times base hot days.
entries.verifierProblem: The researcher's range [0.054, 0.221] held the Barreca ratio at its central value, but that ratio is the largest uncertainty: its numerator is not significant, so the ratio runs [0, 0.32] and the range is [0, 0.30] at the central D&G value ([0, 0.49] with D&G's own CI). The ratio also divides a Panel B coefficient (high of 90-99F, night bin held fixed) by a Panel A coefficient (mean above 90F, against 40-79F), so it is a cross-specification estimate. The researcher's caveat that the effect is 'similar in counties above and below the median' (0.892 against 1.020) is overstated: the below-median estimate has SE 7.138 (95% CI about -13 to +15), so it cannot support similarity or linearity. Page fixes: the '0.94' sentence is on page 167, and the energy quote is on page 154, not 153.
entries.caveats: SOURCED for days with a mean above 90F (0.936 per 100,000, 0.11%) and ESTIMATED for the game's high-of-90F measure through the Barreca ratio. D&G is about 3.7 times Barreca for the same kind of day (0.936 per 100,000 against 0.0034 x 73.82 = 0.251), because D&G uses an annual model that nets out short-term displacement differently and a 50-60F reference instead of 40-79F; treat the two entries as the spread. For the link's group (older people), the 65+ coefficient is 5.219 per 100,000 (SE 1.416, 95% CI 2.44-8.00), 5.6 times the all-age figure. Energy side: the same paper (page 154) finds one more day above 90F 'leads to a 0.4 percent increase in annual consumption', relevant to energy-price-to-ac-use.

The JPE (2016) abstract was read on IDEAS (https://ideas.repec.org/a/ucp/jpolec/doi10.1086-684582.html).
entries.quote: "The estimates in columns (2b) and (3b) suggest that each 10 percentage point increase in residential AC ownership is associated with a decrease in the mortality effect of >90 °F days by 0.002 log points; this is roughly 10 percent of the effect of a >90 °F day in the pre-1960 period. Thus, the regressions imply that an increase in AC coverage from 0% to 59% (which is the average share of the population with residential AC in the 1960-2004 period) reduces the effect of >90°F days on log monthly mortality rates by 0.0132 (=0.59*-0.0223)." Table 6: "Number of Days Above 90 ° F × Share with Residential AC ... -0.0223*** -0.0217** (0.0056) (0.0067)". Table 3 Panel A: "Number of Days Above 90°F 0.0092** 0.0216*** 0.0034*** (0.0028) (0.0029) (0.0009)". Table 7, Age 65+: "-0.0273** (0.0093)". JPE abstract (IDEAS): "First, the mortality impact of days with mean temperature exceeding 80°F declined by 75 percent."
entries.linkUnit: The heat-to-deaths moderator on housing.ac-share, effectAtFull in the default 'scale' mode. The web applies moderatorScale = 1 + effectAtFull x level (src/core2/outcome-web-model.ts, no floor in 'scale' mode), and level is housing.ac-share as stored, in whole percents (US 89; src/core2/modules/outcome-web.ts causeAt reads it raw). So the value is per whole percent of AC share.
entries.conversion: 1) delta = -0.0223 (SE 0.0056): the change in a day-above-90F's effect on log monthly mortality per unit of AC share (0 to 1), 1960-2004. 2) The no-AC effect is the 1931-1959 coefficient, 0.0216 (SE 0.0029). 3) delta / no-AC effect = -0.0223 / 0.0216 = -1.03 per unit share, so full AC removes about all of the hot-day excess; the 95% CI of delta, [-0.0333, -0.0113], gives [-1.54, -0.52]. 4) The web reads the share in whole percents, so per point this is -0.0103 (CI -0.0154 to -0.0052). 5) Cap (required, verifier): at -0.0103 the places at 97% AC get a factor of -0.001, which would make hot days save lives, and drift lets the share reach 99.5%; at -0.0100 the factor at 99.5% is 0.005. The CI's lower end, -0.0154, goes negative above 65% AC (most places), so the usable range is [-0.0100, -0.0052] and the value is -0.0100. 6) Because the scale is absolute, not relative to the place's base AC, the size it multiplies must be the zero-AC effect: with the cap, 0.0369 / (1 - 0.59) = 0.090 per 100,000 per hot day. At today's US 89% the factor is 1 - 0.0100 x 89 = 0.11, which leaves about 0.010 per 100,000 per hot day.
entries.verifierProblem: The researcher reported -1.03 (range [-1.54, -0.52]) per unit share, but the link reads housing.ac-share in whole percents, so the value must be entered per point (-0.0103), and the cap at full protection is required, not optional: at -0.0103 places at 97% AC get a negative factor, and the CI's lower end goes negative above 65% AC. Corrected value -0.0100, range [-0.0100, -0.0052]. With the cap the derived figures shift: zero-AC size 0.090 (not 0.094) and factor at 89% 0.11 (not 0.081). The baseline is also inconsistent: with no-AC effect 0.0216 the linear model predicts 0.0216 x (1 - 1.03 x 0.59) = 0.0085 for 1960-2004, but Table 3 prints 0.0034; taking the 1960-2004 zero-AC effect instead (0.0034 + 0.59 x 0.0223 = 0.0166) gives -1.34 per unit share, full protection at 75% AC, which is more reason to cap.
entries.caveats: The value is the ratio of two printed coefficients from different samples (delta from 1960-2004, the no-AC effect from 1931-1959), so it is ESTIMATED. The linear form probably overstates protection at high AC: footnote 35 shows the AC interaction shrinking by decade ('1960-69: -0.0484 (0.0098), 1970-79: -0.0337 (0.0105), 1980-89: -0.0294 (0.0049), 1990-04: -0.0213 (0.0033)'). The moderator is stronger for people 65 and over (-0.0273, SE 0.0093) and for Black residents (-0.0474 against -0.0197 for whites); infants are -0.0230 (SE 0.0170), not significant. The row's current anchor ('about 75%') is the JPE abstract's decline for days above 80F, not the AC coefficient; the paper says AC 'explains essentially the entire decline'. Design risk: if health.heat-deaths is a proportional outcome whose base already includes today's AC, an absolute moderator understates every change by about 1 / 0.11 = 9 times at 89% AC (12 times uncapped). Either keep the outcome on a 'level' scale with the zero-AC size 0.090, or make the moderator relative to the place's base AC. This is also why energy-price-to-ac-use, which moves housing.ac-share, feeds this link.

entries.citation: Doremus, Jacqz and Johnston, 'Sweating the energy bill: Extreme weather, poor households, and the energy spending gap', Journal of Environmental Economics and Management 112 (2022), doi 10.1016/j.jeem.2022.102609. Abstract read on IDEAS (https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/jeeman/v112y2022ics0095069622000018.html). entries.quote: JEEM abstract (IDEAS): "low-income households' energy spending is half as responsive to extreme temperatures". Working paper: "Replacing a temperate day with a very hot day (> 30C/> 86F) increases electricity spending for higher-income households by 0.5 percent but does not increase electricity spending for low-income households." Footnote 22: "This calculation uses the estimated coefficients on the over 30 bins from column (3) of Table 2 (0.00536 and -0.00509) and assumes 30 days per month." Appendix C: "Our main specification implies that higher-income households increase their daily electricity spending by 16.1 percent if a temperate day is replaced with a day over 30C, while low-income households increase their daily spending by only 0.8 percent." Section 6.1: "For electricity, we find a one kWh increase in use is associated with a $0.105 increase in spending for low-income households, compared to a $0.111 increase for higher-income households."
entries.linkUnit: From energy.electricity-price (cents per kWh, all customers, EIA 2024, US 12.94) to housing.ac-share (percent of homes using AC, RECS 2020), shape linear, per 'price' (read as per cent per kWh), lagMonths 0.
entries.conversion: No conversion is possible: the paper does not estimate a price response (its state-by-month and month-year fixed effects absorb seasonal state price levels and national shocks), and it shows that low- and higher-income households pay about the same per kWh ($0.105 against $0.111). What it does size is the income gap in hot-day AC use. On a day with a mean above 30C (86F), electricity spending (inverse hyperbolic sine, about a percentage change of the monthly bill) rises 0.00536 for higher-income households and 0.00536 - 0.00509 = 0.00027 for households under 1.5 times the poverty line, so the low-income response is 0.00027 / 0.00536 = 5% of others'. The 95% CI of the gap is -0.005 +/- 1.96 x 0.002 = [-0.0089, -0.0011]. The paper reads this as low-income households not running AC they have because of the bill (credit constraints), not as a price effect.
entries.caveats: This study does not size this link. It fits as a 'varies' on income for hot-day AC use, for example on heat-to-deaths' AC moderator, where homes that own AC but cannot afford to run it give less protection. Any such weight needs its spread: the gap's CI puts the low-income share of the response anywhere from below 0 to (0.00536 - 0.0011) / 0.00536 = 0.79, so a weight of about 0.05 holds for electricity on hot days only, with spread [0, 0.8]; for total energy spending the paper says 'half as responsive' (Table 2 column 1: 0.005 against -0.003). Its outcome is spending, not AC ownership, and housing.ac-share (RECS) counts homes using AC equipment at all, which a month's bill barely moves. The survey's smallestBuild option to grade the link as covered by a price elasticity in place-prices stands, with its double-count risk: if place-prices gains an electricity quantity response, AC rationing is already inside it. The numbers come from the 2021 working paper; the published JEEM tables were not read and may differ.

entries.conversion: 1) The paper bins each day's CO against the 9 ppm standard: 0-25% (0-2.25 ppm, the omitted base), 25-50% (2.25-4.5), 50-75% (4.5-6.75), 75-100% (6.75-9) and over 100% (over 9). Each coefficient is the change in the share of days absent when all of a period's days fall in that bin; footnote 13 lets it be read per day. 2) The two top bins: 6.75-9 ppm gives +0.0500, 95% CI [0.0273, 0.0727]; over 9 ppm gives +0.0891, CI [0.0475, 0.1307]. 3) As a proportion of the 3.58% baseline: a 6.75-9 ppm day is 0.0500/0.0358 = +1.40, CI [0.76, 2.03]; a day over 9 ppm is +2.49, CI [1.33, 3.65]. 4) Below 6.75 ppm the exposure bins are zero or negative (-0.0018, SE 0.0017; -0.0110, SE 0.0056), so the effect is a step at about 75% of the standard, not a line. 5) Threshold shape at = 6.75 ppm, ramp drawn through the 6.75-9 bin midpoint, 7.875 ppm (1.125 ppm over): 1.40 / 1.125 = 1.24 per ppm above 6.75, CI [0.68, 1.81]. At 9 ppm the ramp gives 2.79 (0.0999 absolute), inside the over-9 bin's CI; optionally set steeperAt 9 with steeperExtraSize -1.24 to flatten it at the standard. 6) Range (verifier's correction): with Table 5's leads and lags the current 75-100% coefficient falls to 0.0324 (0.0127), so the same-day ramp is 0.0324/0.0358/1.125 = 0.80 per ppm, CI [0.19, 1.42]; the range covering both specifications is [0.19, 1.81]. 7) A linear shape from zero is not recommended: from the base-bin midpoint 1.125 ppm to 7.875 ppm it gives 0.207 per ppm (CI [0.113, 0.301]) and overstates every level below 6.75 ppm, where the paper finds nothing. 8) Lag: the coefficient is a cumulative effect within a six-week attendance block (the paper: the aggregation 'precludes identification of the precise timing of pollutant effects'); reading it per day is footnote 13's stated assumption, and lagMonths 0 holds for the immediate effect.
entries.caveats: The bin coefficients are SOURCED; the per-ppm ramp is derived from them, so it is ESTIMATED. Make-up absences (verifier): Table 5 adds one- and two-period leads and lags, and the one-period lag is negative (75-100%: -0.0346 (0.0119); over-75%: current 0.0367 (0.0125), lag -0.0394 (0.0124)); the paper says parents 'whose children were absent in the last period try to avoid absences in the current period'. So the extra absences are largely made up in the next six weeks (net over about 12 weeks: 0.0367 - 0.0394 = about -0.003), and a same-day stay-home term with no later pull back would overstate a year's absences. Drawing the ramp through the bin midpoint assumes days spread evenly across 6.75-9 ppm; if they bunch near 6.75, the slope is steeper, and the CI omits this. The 50-75% bin (-0.0110, SE 0.0056) has t = 1.96, borderline significantly negative. Such days were rare even in the paper's sample (Table 2: 0.0003-0.0015 of days in the 6.75-9 bin, 0.0000-0.0002 over 9 ppm), so the sample-average effect was about 0.00006, about 0.2% of absences; the large case the paper names is El Paso (16 days over and 19 in 75-100% in 1986, 1 and 6 in 2001, which the paper says cut absences by 0.8 percentage points). The reading must be a daily maximum ('maximum level for the day' is the working paper's wording, p. 16); a monthly or annual place average never comes near 6.75 ppm, so on such an average the link reads zero. One state only, schools within 10 miles of one of 20-24 CO monitors. Read point per the survey: schoolDay, src/core2/modules/school.ts.

entries.conversion: 1) Table 3's dependent variable is the yield spread over a coupon-equivalent Treasury, 'measured in percentage points'. 2) Closure coefficient = 0.0549 percentage points x 100 = 5.49 bp per closure, about 5.5. 3) SE = 0.0549/4.44 = 0.01236 pp = 1.24 bp. 4) 95% CI = 5.49 +/- 1.96 x 1.24 = [3.07, 7.91] bp, about [3.1, 7.9]. 5) Against the closure county's own preclosure gap it is 0.0566 pp = 5.7 bp (t 4.47). 6) The abstract's 5-11 bp spans specifications: secondary yields, all bonds 6.4 bp (t 3.99); revenue bonds, offering 10.6 bp (t 5.05, CI [6.5, 14.7]); counties with few newspapers 10.3 bp. Use 5.5 for a government's general borrowing. 7) Lag (verifier's correction): the 5.5 coefficient is defined only from 36 months after the closure (months 0-35 are coded neither Closure nor PreClosure), so lagMonths 36 matches it. 8) In dollars, 5.5 bp x $65 million average issue x 10-year average duration = $357,500 per issue; the paper's own figure is $650,000 for 10 bp.
entries.caveats: Lag: the researcher proposed lagMonths 12 at the full 5.5 bp; that overstates years one to three by about 1-2 bp. The one-year '6 basis points' comes from Internet Appendix Table A-3 (not fetched), whose three-year definition gives 9.5 bp, a different specification from Table 3; within A-3 one year is 6/9.5 = 63% of the three-year size and two years 7.4/9.5 = 78%, which scaled to Table 3 is about 3.5 bp at 12 months and 4.3 bp at 24 months. Use the A-3 windows (6, 7.4, 9.5, 10 and 9.6 bp at 1-5 years) for timing only, never size; keep lag 12 only if the row says so. Form: Closure is a 0/1 indicator per county, and a 'closure' is a county-year fall in the number of dailies, including a paper going nondaily (152 of the 296 drop-outs); the paper never measured a second closure in the same county, so cap the link at one closure per county (or use a saturating shape), and count a paper going nondaily as a closure if the press module records that. The effect depends on how many papers are left: 10.3 bp in low-newspaper counties, while a closure in a high-newspaper county 'has no significant effect'. What was measured: 204 closures, 1996-2015, of daily newspapers in counties that had at most 3 dailies before; the outcome is the offering yield of all municipal issuers in the closure county (counties, cities, districts), not a state's bonds. Per the survey row, the state's interestFactor should exclude this link, and county and city treasuries should read it on their own interest lines; applying one closure to both carries a county-measured spread onto city bonds. If the lead prefers the abstract's spread to the coefficient's CI, use [5, 11]; that widening comes from specification choice, not sampling error. Table 3's caption says columns 1 and 2 are 'secondary and offering ... respectively', but the column header and the text make column 1 the offering yield. Size = the proportional change in the outcome per unit of the cause, with one unit of hostility read as one public attack on a named outlet that the person heard (the experiment's single exposure).
entries.conversion: 1) 'This group' is Republican voters, and the attacker was a Republican politician from the respondent's own state (supplement Table A3), so these are the attacker's co-partisans, the link's group. 2) Change in the share calling the outlet trustworthy: 0.43 - 0.74 = -0.31. 3) Proportional change: -0.31 / 0.74 = -0.419 per attack. 4) Interval (derived, not printed): Republicans are 0.39 of 3,653 (Table A1) = 1,425, split by the arm sizes (1,814 control, 1,839 treatment; Table A7) into about 707 and 717; SE of the difference = sqrt(0.74 x 0.26/707 + 0.43 x 0.57/717) = 0.0248; 95% CI of the difference = [-0.359, -0.261], divided by 0.74 = [-0.485, -0.353]. 5) Size -0.419 per unit of hostility, range [-0.485, -0.353], for trust in the attacked outlet among the attacker's supporters.
entries.caveats: (a) The study measures trust in the attacked local paper, not general trust in the media (the Gallup measure press.media-trust uses now); supplement Table G1 finds no spillover to CNN (see the spillover entry), so the link should be re-pointed at trust in the attacked outlet, as the survey row says (trustOf/trustWeight in src/core2/modules/news.ts). (b) Trust was measured in the same survey session as the attack, so the lag is 0; no persistence was measured, and the row's 3-month lag and any decay are unmeasured: register the persistence as a stopgap. (c) Under a linear read about 2.4 attacks (1 / 0.419) would take trust to zero, so read hostility as 0 to 1 (whether the person heard an attack in the window) or cap it. (d) Refinement from the replication data (verifier): 'trustworthy' is trust5 >= 3 (at least 'somewhat suitable'); Republicans (n 724 control, 698 treatment) go from 0.7445 to 0.4255, -31.9 points, relative -0.428, delta-method 95% CI [-0.483, -0.374]; -0.419 is the rounded-input version. At the stricter cutoff (>= 4, closer to Gallup's 'great deal/fair amount') Republicans go from 0.366 to 0.175, relative -0.52, so a range down to about -0.52 covers the choice of cutoff. (e) Other groups, settled from the data: the release's 'Democrats became 7% less trusting' is relative (0.896 to 0.832, -6.4 points, -7.2%), and its independents 'fell by 28%' is about points (0.713 to 0.439, -27.4 points, -38.5% relative; n 115/139). (f) Only attacks by Republicans were tested; the same size for a Democratic attacker's supporters is an assumption the authors note but did not test. (g) press.media-trust has no base, so it uses the proportional scale (1 + effect, floored at 0 in webReach). (h) The row's current source, Ladd 2012, was not fetched.

entries.conversion: 1) Larceny rise = +128.94 per 100,000 per year, SE 43.27 (Table 5, first column). 2) Pre-reform base = the state's 2014 larceny rate, 1,527.80 per 100,000 (Appendix Table A2). 3) Percent change in larceny = 128.94 / 1,527.80 = +8.44%; 95% CI = (128.94 +/- 1.96 x 43.27) / 1,527.80 = [44.13, 213.75] / 1,527.80 = [+2.89%, +13.99%]. 4) Share of crime.property that is larceny: other theft is 79.3 of 97.6 property victimizations per 1,000 households (BJS Criminal Victimization 2024, table 2; see the BJS entry) = 0.8125. 5) Size = 0.0844 x 0.8125 = 0.0686 per law in force; range [0.0289, 0.1399] x 0.8125 = [0.0235, 0.1137].
entries.caveats: The authors stress that estimates depend on method; for several estimators more than half of the relative rise in property crime is 'driven by a decline in the counterfactual crime rate rather than increases for California' (that sentence is about property crime, not larceny specifically). Other larceny numbers in the paper: the synthetic cohort gives '124 and136 incidents per 100,000' (+8.1% to +8.9%); the Table 4 2015-16 difference-in-differences is 144.62 to 153.16 with placebo p 0.24 (+9.5% to +10.0%); the cross-county analysis gives 'a 3.1 percent increase in larceny theft'; the first twelve months against the prediction give 193.85 (+12.7%). The break is at implementation (t=0), so the measured lag is about 0 months; the row's 3 months is a conservative delay. The share in step 4 also scales burglary, which Prop 47 did not change (the survey row's risk); a separate larceny measure would remove that. UCR larceny includes commercial theft such as shoplifting, which the household NCVS does not count; PPIC says thefts from motor vehicles (household theft the NCVS counts) were about three quarters of the rise, so the share scaling is approximate.

entries.quote: Despite this sensitivity, there is evidence from all methods that larceny theft increase with, a ballpark summary of 5 percent roughly consistent with the totality of our analysis.

entries.conversion: As corrected by the verifier. 1) The '5 percent' sentence (Section 7) follows the property-crime ranges in the same paragraph (0-3% cross-county, 5-7.5% synthetic cohort, 6-10% time series), and the abstract's parallel sentence says property crime rose by 'a ballpark summary of five to seven percent'; so 5% summarizes property crime, not larceny. 2) The paper's larceny-specific estimates are 3.1%, 8.1-10.0% and 8.4-12.7%, which no reading centers on 5%. 3) Reading the abstract's property 5-7% (2014 base 2,441.7) as mostly larceny gives 122-171 per 100,000, which is 8.0-11.2% of 1,527.8, or 0.065-0.091 in crime.property, in line with Table 5. 4) Recommended: center 0.0686 (Table 5), range [0, 0.1137]: the floor is 0 because Bartos and Kubrin's placebo tests cannot rule out a zero effect, and the top is the Table 5 95% CI top, 13.99% x 0.8125. 5) The researcher's 0.05 x 0.8125 = 0.0406 is kept only as a low alternative, labeled the property-crime ballpark.
entries.verifierProblem: The researcher read the '5 percent' ballpark as a larceny figure and proposed 0.0406. The quote is in Section 7 (Discussion), not the abstract, and the 5% summarizes the paper's property-crime ranges; its larceny estimates (3.1%, 8.1-10.0%, 8.4-12.7%) do not center on 5%. Corrected value 0.0686 (Table 5), range [0, 0.1137]; 0.0406 survives only as a low alternative.
entries.caveats: This replaces the row's +9% center (0.0731, the 2018 PPIC report) with the authors' 2019 Table 5 estimate, and narrows the range from the current 0.1463 (0.18 larceny, which is no study's interval but 'the default contested range from none to twice the size') to 0.1137, a real CI top.

entries.conversion: The abstract gives no number. It shows that a zero effect cannot be ruled out under the placebo tests, so the lower end of the range is 0 (in larceny and in crime.property alike: 0 x 0.8125 = 0). The upper end comes from the Dominguez-Rivera, Lofstrom and Raphael Table 5 CI, not from this paper.
entries.caveats: No point size is quoted because the abstract prints none. The full text (state panel 1970-2015, synthetic control) was not loaded. The same abstract says Prop 47 'had no effect on homicide, rape, aggravated assault, robbery, or burglary', which supports the caveat that crime.property's burglary scaling overstates.

entries.quote: In contrast, the increase in larceny theft is marginally statistically significant.14 We estimate that Prop 47 led to a rise in the larceny theft rate of about 135 per 100,000 residents, an increase of close to 9 percent compared to the 2014 rate (Figure 7). ... 14 Specifically, the increase in larceny theft is significant at the 10 percent significance level.

entries.caveats: Cross-check of the current value only. Significant only at 10%. The same authors' later IZA paper puts the best-identified larceny rise at 8.44% (Table 5). The report also says 'thefts from motor vehicles account for about three-quarters of this increase', which supports the NCVS household mapping.

entries.use: The conversion factor from a change in larceny to a change in crime.property.
entries.citation: Bureau of Justice Statistics, Criminal Victimization, 2024 (NCJ 310547, Sept. 2025), table 2 (property victimizations and rate per 1,000 households, 2024 column).
entries.linkUnit: A conversion factor from a percent change in larceny (other theft) to a proportional change in crime.property, the link's outcome.
entries.conversion: Share = other theft 79.3 / total property 97.6 per 1,000 households (2024, the last pair of columns) = 0.8125. A larceny change x becomes a crime.property change of 0.8125 x x, assuming burglary, trespass and motor vehicle theft are unchanged.
entries.caveats: Matches the row's notes and src/core2/data/crime/victimization.json. In the crime engine both burglary and other-property list crime.property in webMeasures, so the factor scales the full 97.6 total, and the share is the right scaling. The NCVS counts victimizations, while the FBI counts reported offenses; a share is fine for scaling a proportional change. Footnote e defines other theft as taking 'without personal contact with the victim' from households, while UCR larceny also counts commercial theft, so the mapping is approximate.
